prompt: Sort each incident under the leg of the CIA triad it primarily attacks.
hints: Name the property the attacker destroyed, not the technology they used. The same technology shows up as a control on one side and a weapon on the other.
If two legs seem to fit, ask which loss the victim notices first, and which one they could still be suffering without knowing.
items: Ransomware encrypts the file server
Firmware replaced with a tampered build
Botnet floods the public website with traffic
Customer database exfiltrated and posted online
Payroll figures silently altered in the database
Attacker reads unencrypted traffic on public Wi-Fi

prompt: A hospital must keep patient records reachable through any disruption — outage, attack or accident. Select every control below that primarily protects AVAILABILITY.
items: DDoS mitigation service
Digital signatures on lab results
Full-disk encryption
Offline immutable backups
Redundant failover servers
Role-based access control
TLS on the web portal
Tested restore procedure

prompt: Sort each measure under the property it primarily provides.
hints: Ask what each measure exists *for*: establishing who someone is, making an action undeniable afterwards, or holding less data in the first place.
Several of these produce a side effect that belongs to a different bucket. Sort by the reason the measure was put there, not by everything it happens to help with.
items: Unlocking a workstation with a registered fingerprint
Collecting only the data fields the service actually needs
Keeping a tamper-evident audit log of who changed each record
Requiring a password plus a one-time code from the user's phone
Honouring a customer's request to erase what you hold about them
Digitally signing an approved payment so it traces to one named employee

prompt: For each sign-in step, decide which factor category it draws on. Ask what an attacker would have to get hold of: something stored only in your memory, a specific enrolled device, or a measurement of your body. A code is not a memory factor just because it can be read out — what was enrolled is the device that generates it.
items: The master passphrase that unlocks your password manager
A fingerprint the reader matches against an enrolled scan
An iris pattern the door camera measures against a stored template
A signing key that never leaves the TPM chip soldered to your laptop
A rotating code read from an authenticator app registered to one handset
The answer to the security question you chose when you opened the account

prompt: Sort each control by its TYPE — how it does its job. Ignore when it acts; that is its function, not its type.
hints: Ask what actually does the enforcing: a machine, a rule that people follow, or a barrier in the physical world.
A control can be preventive or detective and still be any of the three types. Type and function are separate questions — answer the one being asked.
items: A locked door on the server room
Full-disk encryption on every laptop
A perimeter fence around the data centre
A firewall filtering inbound traffic by rule
Background checks run before a new hire starts
An acceptable-use policy signed by every employee

prompt: A new branch office is opening. Select every safeguard on the plan that is an ADMINISTRATIVE control.
items: A badge-operated turnstile in the lobby
A mandatory data-classification scheme staff must apply to new documents
A safe for storing backup tapes
A written incident response procedure
Annual security awareness training for all staff
Antivirus deployed to every endpoint
Separation of duties on payment approvals
TLS on the customer web portal

prompt: Each situation is most directly about one canon's subject matter: public safety and the infrastructure (I), your own honesty and legality (II), what you owe the client who hired you (III), or the standing of the profession (IV). Sort them. Note that ranking settles conflicts of *duty* — it is not how you classify what a situation is about.
hints: Ask who is primarily being protected: the public, your own integrity, the client who hired you, or the profession itself.
More than one canon can be true of the same act. Ask which one the situation is fundamentally *about*, not which others it also touches.
buckets: Canon I — protect society and the infrastructure
Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
items: You refuse to scan a network you have no written authorisation to test
You report a peer who is selling leaked ISC2 exam questions to candidates
You report a vulnerability you found in a city's emergency dispatch system
You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
You spend an afternoon each month mentoring junior analysts with no billable work attached
You turn down a second client whose work would create a conflict of interest with your current engagement
You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
A vendor ignores your reports of a medical-device firmware flaw while patients remain at risk, and you keep pressing for a fix

prompt: Sort each decision under the risk treatment it represents.
items: Enforce MFA on all remote access
Roll out full-disk encryption on every laptop
Discontinue the legacy file-sharing service entirely
Buy a cyber-insurance policy covering breach response costs
Add a clause making the hosting provider financially responsible for data loss
Document the remaining chance of a laptop stolen while unlocked, and have the head of IT sign it off

prompt: Sort each document or statement into the governance layer it belongs to.
hints: Work down in order: is it imposed on you from outside, is it optional, and does it state an intention, a specific requirement, or a sequence of actions?
Force and specificity are two separate axes. Something can be mandatory and vague, or detailed and optional — the pair of answers picks the layer.
items: Data at rest must be encrypted with AES-256
Where practical, prefer a passphrase of four or more words
All production servers must run the approved hardened OS image
HIPAA's requirements for safeguarding protected health information
The organisation will protect the confidentiality of all customer data
Every system must have a named owner who is accountable for its security
Step 1: open the admin console. Step 2: select Enrol device. Step 3: scan the QR code
To report a suspected phishing email, click Report, then forward it to the security inbox
